must_find.description: DROP COLUMN destroys the legacy total on deploy, with nothing copied out first.
The projection increments on every delivery and tracks no applied events, so a redelivery or a replay inflates the totals.

acceptable.description: down() adds the column back empty, so a rollback is structural only.

must_not_flag.description: Claiming the migration has no down or cannot be reverted. It has one and it restores the column; what it cannot restore is the data, which is a different and more precise point.

Claiming DROP COLUMN fails when the table already has rows. It does not - that is the NOT NULL rule from sample-02, applied to a different statement. The real problem is that the drop succeeds and takes the data with it.
Treating the read model lagging behind the write model as a defect. That is the design of a projection, not a bug in it.
Demanding the ORM's query builder instead of raw SQL inside an infrastructure adapter. The rubric allows raw SQL there.

notes: The second redelivery case, deliberately unlike sample-02 and sample-04: no broker retry in sight, the replay that rebuilds a read model is the trigger, and the damage is a wrong number rather than wrong stock. Also the set's first sample where the tempting wrong answer is stated as a must_not_flag - the migration does have a down(), and saying it does not is a more attractive finding than the true one. No deterministic analyzer fires anywhere in this sample, so both must_find items are the model's to earn: the projection sits in infrastructure, where using the ORM is correct, and the migration neither adds a NOT NULL column nor leaves down() empty.
